title: How Stuttering Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain stuttering (called stammering in the UK and disfluency by scientists). They cover what counts as disfluent speech, the three interruption types (repetition, prolongation, block), prevalence (about one percent of adults, five percent of children, most children outgrow it, more males than females), genetic evidence from twin studies, developmental versus acquired and psychogenic stuttering, Barry Guitar's five stages of severity, the brain and dopamine research, the Moses story, historical treatments (Demosthenes, frenulum surgery, Mendelssohn, Erasmus Darwin, Sanson), advice for parents and listeners, fluency through singing and unison speech and the delayed-auditory-feedback style device, Porky Pig's voice actor Joe Doherty, and famous people who stutter. The episode ends with a listener mail about a Chicago show and a road trip playlist.

segments.title: Opening banter and defining stuttering
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the topic, note the names stuttering, stammering and disfluency, and discuss how disfluency is normal speech interruption that becomes stuttering at the far end of the spectrum. They also discuss how they handle disfluency in their own show.

segments.title: Attention, shame, and accepting a stutter
segments.summary: The hosts explain that stuttering is an interruption of communication, not a sign of low intelligence, and that attention to it can worsen it. They discuss the three interruption types (repetition, prolongation, block), personal experience, a blog post by Danny Litwack about accepting his stutter, and how people with stutters hide triggers like certain letters.

segments.title: Prevalence and genetics
segments.summary: Roughly one percent of adults stutter, versus about five percent of children, most of whom outgrow it. Men stutter more than women. Twin studies suggest a genetic basis, with a higher concordance in identical twins than fraternal twins.

segments.title: Developmental, acquired, and psychogenic stuttering
segments.summary: The hosts describe the main categories: developmental stuttering (most cases), acquired stuttering from causes like head trauma, Parkinson's, or medication, and the claimed psychogenic type. They then tell the story of a man who quit stuttering after taking psychedelic mushrooms up a tree and later became a mycologist.

segments.title: Childhood onset, Barry Guitar's levels, and dopamine
segments.summary: Stuttering in children often appears and resolves within about eighteen months, and becomes more entrenched with age. Speech pathologists look at severity using Barry Guitar's five levels and co-occurring symptoms. The hosts discuss dopamine's possible role and the brain's separate language processing and articulation regions, and that research into genes linked to cellular trafficking proteins is early.

segments.title: Moses and historical theories and treatments
segments.summary: The hosts recount the story of Moses being given a bowl of hot coals and a stutter, and his request to God, who assigned Aaron to speak. They discuss the debate over whether Moses had a lisp. They then cover historical treatments: Demosthenes' pebbles and walking speech, Amida's frenulum surgery and tongue slicing, and the theories of Moses Mendelssohn, Erasmus Darwin, and Sanson.

segments.title: Parenting advice and speaking with people who stutter
segments.summary: The hosts review advice for parents: give children time to talk, maintain eye contact, avoid telling them to slow down or think before speaking, model slow speech, be honest, and focus on content not delivery. They also discuss how to talk with adults who stutter, avoiding finishing their sentences, and that stutters are worse in high-anxiety situations like job interviews.

segments.title: Treatments: singing, unison speech, and devices
segments.summary: The hosts discuss that people who stutter often speak fluently when singing or speaking in unison, and a device that plays back the speaker's voice with a slight delay, which helped in clinical settings but is not well tested outside them. They mention country singer Mel Tillis, who stuttered.

segments.title: Famous people who stutter
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Porky Pig, whose original voice actor Joe Doherty stuttered and was later replaced, with the stutter kept in the character. They then list famous people who stutter or stuttered, including James Earl Jones, Emily Blunt, Samuel L. Jackson, Winston Churchill, Joe Biden, and Kendrick Lamar.

segments.title: Listener mail: Chicago show and Water Slides
segments.summary: A listener writes about a road trip from Chicago to Wisconsin Dells with a ten-year-old using a playlist of episodes, including How Water Slides Work, which is one of the show's highest-performing episodes. The listener mentions attending a Chicago show.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners, invite contact via Twitter, Facebook, and email, and point to the website for more information.
